Pythagorean theorem: In a right triangle the square of the hypotenuse (the side opposite the right angle) equals the sum of the squares of the legs: a^2 + b^2 = c^2. It is used to find missing sides, distances and diagonals. Whole-number triples such as 3-4-5, 5-12-13, 8-15-17 and 7-24-25 are called Pythagorean triples. The converse tells you whether a triangle is right, acute or obtuse by comparing c^2 with a^2 + b^2.
Special right triangles: Two right triangles have fixed side ratios. The 45-45-90 triangle (half of a square) has sides x, x and x times the square root of 2. The 30-60-90 triangle (half of an equilateral triangle) has sides x, x times the square root of 3 and 2x, where x is the shorter leg opposite the 30 degree angle. Knowing these ratios lets you find sides without the Pythagorean theorem.
Sine, cosine and tangent: For an acute angle in a right triangle the trigonometric ratios compare sides: sine = opposite / hypotenuse, cosine = adjacent / hypotenuse and tangent = opposite / adjacent (memory aid SOH-CAH-TOA). Opposite and adjacent depend on which angle you are using. The ratio depends only on the angle, not the size of the triangle. Sine of an angle equals the cosine of its complement, and a calculator must be in degree mode.
Solving right triangles: To solve a right triangle means to find all missing sides and angles. Use the Pythagorean theorem or trigonometric ratios to find sides, and use inverse trigonometric functions (sin^-1, cos^-1, tan^-1) to find angles from sides. Applications include angles of elevation and depression, which are measured from the horizontal.
Law of sines and cosines: For any triangle (not only right ones) with sides a, b, c opposite angles A, B, C, the Law of Sines says a / sin A = b / sin B = c / sin C. Use it for ASA, AAS and SSA cases (SSA can be ambiguous). The Law of Cosines says c^2 = a^2 + b^2 - 2ab cos C. Use it for SAS (two sides and the included angle) and SSS. It reduces to the Pythagorean theorem when C is 90 degrees.
